questions.passage: The morning of the race, Kenji's stomach felt like it was full of butterflies. He had trained for six months, waking up before dawn three times a week. At the starting line, he spotted his rival, Marcus, who had beaten him at every previous meet. Kenji closed his eyes, took a slow breath, and told himself he had done the work. When the gun fired, his legs moved almost before he thought about it.
questions.text: Which detail from the passage BEST supports the inference that Kenji was well-prepared?
options: He saw Marcus at the starting line.
He had trained for six months, waking up before dawn three times a week.
His stomach felt like it was full of butterflies.
He closed his eyes before the race began.
questions.explanation: The specific detail about six months of early-morning training directly supports the inference that Kenji prepared seriously for the race.

questions.passage: Rosa had always been the fastest reader in class, and she was proud of it. When the school book-fair competition asked students to read the most books, she tore through them as fast as she could — even skimming the last chapters. When her teacher asked her to discuss her favorite book from the list, Rosa realized she could barely remember any of them. That night, she picked up a short novel and read it slowly, savoring each page.
questions.text: What is the theme of this passage?
options: Reading competitions are unfair.
Speed and understanding are not the same thing.
Teachers should not ask students hard questions.
Short books are better than long books.
questions.explanation: Rosa learns that racing through books left her with no real understanding or enjoyment; the theme is that genuine reading requires time and attention, not just speed.

questions.passage: The old lighthouse keeper, Mr. Aldous, had lived on the rocky point for forty years. The walls of his cottage were lined with maps and weather charts. Every evening, no matter how cold or foggy, he climbed the 112 steps to the lamp room and polished the lens until it gleamed. He said the light was not for him — it was for the sailors who had no one else to trust.
questions.text: What details from the passage show that Mr. Aldous was dedicated to his duty?
options: He collected maps and charts as a hobby.
He climbed the stairs and polished the lens every evening, no matter the weather, for forty years.
He chose to live in a cottage instead of a house.
He trusted sailors more than he trusted townspeople.
questions.explanation: Polishing the lens every evening regardless of weather, for forty years, shows deep dedication; these specific details from the text support that characterization.

questions.passage: When Amara walked into the gymnasium for the first time, she felt like a tiny fish in a very large ocean. The room seemed to stretch forever, and everywhere she looked, older students moved with confidence she could not imagine having.
questions.text: What does the simile 'a tiny fish in a very large ocean' mean in this context?
options: Amara is very small for her age.
Amara feels overwhelmed and out of place.
Amara is a strong swimmer.
Amara is surrounded by many fish.
questions.explanation: The simile compares Amara to a small fish in a vast ocean to convey that she feels insignificant and overwhelmed in the large, unfamiliar gymnasium.

questions.passage: Story A is told by a young girl who is nervous about moving to a new town and leaving her friends behind. Story B is told by that same girl's mother, who is excited about the new job opportunity and a bigger house for the family.
questions.text: How do the two narrators' points of view differ?
options: Both narrators are worried about the move.
Both narrators are excited about the move.
The girl dreads the move; the mother looks forward to it.
The mother is nervous; the girl is happy for her mother.
questions.explanation: The girl's point of view is one of sadness and anxiety about leaving friends, while the mother's point of view is one of excitement about new opportunities.

questions.passage: The monarch butterfly migrates up to 3,000 miles from Canada to Mexico each fall. Scientists have long puzzled over how monarchs navigate such distances. Recent research suggests that monarchs use an internal compass that responds to the Earth's magnetic field, as well as the position of the sun, to find their way south.
questions.text: Based on the passage, what inference can you make about monarch butterflies?
options: Monarch butterflies can only survive in Mexico.
Monarch butterflies have complex navigation abilities.
Scientists fully understand how monarch butterflies migrate.
Monarch butterflies migrate because the sun is too bright in Canada.
questions.explanation: The passage describes monarchs using both a magnetic-field compass and sun position to navigate thousands of miles, supporting the inference that they have sophisticated navigation abilities.

questions.passage: In 1903, Wilbur and Orville Wright tested their flying machine at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. They chose this location because of its steady winds and soft sandy ground. On December 17th, Orville piloted the first successful powered flight, which lasted twelve seconds and covered 120 feet. News of their achievement spread quickly around the world.
questions.text: Why did the Wright brothers choose Kitty Hawk for their test?
options: It was close to their bicycle shop in Ohio.
It had steady winds and soft sandy ground.
It was the only open land available in 1903.
The government required them to test there.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states the brothers chose Kitty Hawk because of its steady winds and soft sandy ground, which were ideal conditions for their test.

questions.passage: Ancient Egyptians used a writing system called hieroglyphics. This system used pictorial symbols to represent words, sounds, or ideas. For centuries, no one could decipher these symbols. Then, in 1799, a stone with the same message carved in three scripts was discovered near the town of Rosetta. Scholars used this stone to finally crack the code.
questions.text: What does the word 'decipher' most likely mean in this passage?
options: To draw or copy symbols carefully.
To create a new writing system.
To figure out the meaning of something difficult to understand.
To destroy ancient artifacts.
questions.explanation: The passage says no one could 'decipher' the symbols, and then scholars used the Rosetta Stone to 'crack the code,' so 'decipher' means to figure out the meaning of something.

questions.passage: Account A (firsthand): 'I was there the day the old bridge collapsed. I heard a loud crack, then the whole thing tilted sideways and fell into the river. People on the bank were screaming.' Account B (secondhand): 'According to city engineers, the bridge's steel cables had been corroding for years. Inspectors had flagged the issue twice, but repairs were never funded.'
questions.text: What does Account B include that Account A does not?
options: A description of the sounds heard at the collapse.
The emotional reaction of the people nearby.
Technical reasons explaining why the bridge fell.
A firsthand description of seeing the bridge fall.
questions.explanation: Account B, the secondhand account from engineers, provides technical background about corroding cables and unfunded repairs, which the eyewitness account does not include.

questions.passage: Recess should be at least 30 minutes long in every school. Studies show that students who have longer recess are better able to focus in class. Physical activity improves memory and attention. Children who play outside also report lower levels of stress. For all these reasons, schools should protect and expand recess time.
questions.text: How does the author support the argument that recess should be at least 30 minutes long?
options: By telling a story about a student who loved recess.
By providing reasons and evidence about focus, memory, and stress.
By listing every school that already has long recess.
By arguing that teachers need a break.
questions.explanation: The author supports the argument with research-based reasons: longer recess improves focus, memory, attention, and reduces stress, all used as evidence for the claim.

questions.text: Which word uses the prefix 'un-' to create a word that means 'not finished'?
options: Undo
Unfinished
Unique
Until
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' means 'not.' Adding it to 'finished' creates 'unfinished,' meaning not finished. 'Undo' means to reverse an action, 'unique' and 'until' do not use 'un-' as a prefix with this meaning.

questions.text: Choose the sentence that correctly uses a relative pronoun.
options: The book when I read last summer was great.
The student who won the award was very surprised.
The park which we go every Sunday is near.
The car whom my dad drives is blue.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the correct relative pronoun to use for a person (the student); 'whom' is for objects, and 'which' and 'when' are used for things and times, not people.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sentence fragment?
options: The team practiced every afternoon after school.
Running as fast as she could through the rain.
My dog barks at every passing car.
We finished the project before the deadline.
questions.explanation: 'Running as fast as she could through the rain' is a fragment because it has no subject and no main verb to complete the thought.

questions.text: Which sentence uses capitalization correctly?
options: Last Summer, our family drove to yellowstone national park.
Last summer, our family drove to Yellowstone National Park.
last summer, our Family drove to Yellowstone national Park.
Last summer, our family drove to yellowstone National Park.
questions.explanation: Proper nouns like 'Yellowstone National Park' must be capitalized; 'summer' is a common noun and is not capitalized in the middle of a sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence conveys the idea most precisely?
options: The dog made a sound and then ran away.
The dog barked loudly at the stranger and sprinted down the alley.
The dog did something and went somewhere fast.
The dog was noisy and then it left.
questions.explanation: Precise words like 'barked loudly,' 'stranger,' and 'sprinted down the alley' paint a clear and specific picture, unlike the vague words in the other options.

questions.passage: The scientist examined the ancient bone fragment with great care. She used a magnifying lens and took meticulous notes, recording every tiny detail she observed.
questions.text: What does 'meticulous' most likely mean based on the context?
options: Quick and careless.
Extremely careful and precise.
Written in a foreign language.
Done without any tools.
questions.explanation: The context clues 'great care,' 'magnifying lens,' and 'recording every tiny detail' all point to 'meticulous' meaning extremely careful and precise.

questions.text: The Latin root 'port' means 'to carry.' What does the word 'transport' most likely mean?
options: To study something carefully.
To carry something across from one place to another.
To build something out of many parts.
To translate words from another language.
questions.explanation: The prefix 'trans-' means 'across' and the root 'port' means 'to carry,' so 'transport' means to carry something from one place to another.

questions.passage: The classroom was a zoo on the last day before winter break. Kids were bouncing off the walls, and even the teacher could not stop smiling.
questions.text: What does the metaphor 'the classroom was a zoo' mean?
options: The classroom had animals in it.
The classroom was chaotic and wild.
The students were studying animals.
The classroom smelled bad.
questions.explanation: Calling the classroom a zoo is a metaphor for chaos and uncontrolled energy; it does not mean there were actual animals, but that the behavior was wild and noisy.

questions.text: Which word is a SYNONYM for 'enormous'?
options: Tiny
Ordinary
Gigantic
Distant
questions.explanation: 'Gigantic' means very large, which is the same meaning as 'enormous'; 'tiny' is an antonym.

questions.passage: For years, Priya's grandfather had told her stories about the village where he grew up. When she finally visited, she expected it to look exactly as he had described. The streets seemed narrower, the houses smaller, and the river was barely a trickle. She felt disappointed — until she sat with her grandfather on the old stone wall and watched him light up as he pointed to the bakery, the schoolhouse, and the path through the field. In that moment, she understood that the place had not shrunk. Her grandfather's love had made it enormous in her memory.
questions.text: What is the central idea of this passage?
options: Old villages are always smaller than people remember.
A place's true size is determined by its buildings.
Love and memory can make ordinary places feel grand and meaningful.
Children should visit their grandparents' hometowns every year.
questions.explanation: The passage concludes that the village had not actually shrunk — her grandfather's love had made it feel enormous in memory, showing how emotion shapes our perception of places.
